values.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
values.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
values.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

What it does

  • It keeps moisture in. A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
  • It suppresses weeds. Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
  • It feeds the soil. Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
  • It protects roots from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
  • It makes a border look finished, which matters more than people admit.

When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

  1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
  2. Water if the soil is dry.
  3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
  4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

values.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
values.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
values.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

  • The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
  • The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
  • The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

How it has settled

Three summers on, the meadow is starting to find its balance. The first year was mostly annual cornfield flowers, as it always is. Since then the perennials have taken over: knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, field scabious and a good deal of yellow rattle, which keeps the grass in check.

We walk down to the bottom most evenings now. We never used to go past the washing line.

Slopes put many people off, but they make some of the most rewarding gardens to design. The changes in level give you views, shelter and a sense of journey that a flat plot cannot.

values.title: We've moved: the new studio on Wharf Lane
values.excerpt: After six years above a bike shop, Northfold now works from a converted joinery workshop by the river.
values.body:
After six years in two rooms above a bike shop, Northfold has a new home. Since the start of the month we have been working from a converted joinery workshop on Wharf Lane, a few minutes' walk from the river.

It is a big change for a small studio, and we wanted to say a little about why we moved and what the new space means for the work.

Why we moved

Honestly, we ran out of room. When there were three of us, two rooms were plenty. Now there are six, plus a growing library of samples, a plan chest, two bicycles and more plants on the windowsills than any landlord would like.

We also wanted somewhere clients could visit. Most of our first meetings happen on site, which is how we like it, but there comes a point in every project where it helps to sit round a big table with the drawings, the samples and the planting lists all out at once. The old studio simply could not do that.

The new space

The workshop dates from the 1890s and was used by a joinery firm until about ten years ago. It has a high timber roof, a long run of north-facing windows that give steady, even light all day, and a yard at the back.

Inside we have:

  • a large shared studio with room for everyone and a little to spare;
  • a meeting room with a table big enough for a full set of plans;
  • a materials wall, with samples of the stone, brick, gravel and timber we use most;
  • a small kitchen, which is already the busiest room in the building.

The yard

The yard is the part we are most excited about. At the moment it is concrete and nettles. Over the next year we are going to turn it into a working garden: a place to trial plants before we use them on projects, test paving and gravel through a northern winter, and grow cut flowers for the studio.

We will share how it goes, including the parts that do not work.

Come and see us

We are planning a small open afternoon in the spring, once the yard has something growing in it. Clients, past and present, neighbours and anyone curious will be welcome. We will post the date here nearer the time.

In the meantime, if you are passing and the door is open, do come in. The kettle is usually on.

values.title: Pruning in late winter: what to cut and what to leave
values.excerpt: Late winter is pruning season for a good share of the garden. How we decide what to cut now, and what to leave alone.
values.body:
Late winter is pruning season for a good share of the garden. The sap is not yet rising, the shape of each plant is easy to see, and there is not much else to do outside. But it is also when the most damage gets done with secateurs, usually with the best intentions.

Here is how we decide what to cut now, and what to leave alone.

Cut now

  • Late-flowering clematis (the ones that flower from midsummer on). Cut every stem back to a pair of fat buds about thirty centimetres above the ground. It feels brutal. They love it.
  • Buddleja, lavatera and hardy fuchsias. These flower on new growth, so a hard cut now gives you more flowers later.
  • Dogwoods and willows grown for their stems. Cut all or a third of the stems to the base, depending on how much colour you want next winter.
  • Apples and pears, if they are free-standing. Take out dead, crossing and inward-facing branches and aim for an open, goblet shape.
  • Wisteria, for its second prune of the year. Shorten the side shoots you cut back in summer to two or three buds.

Leave alone

  • Anything that flowers in spring, such as forsythia, flowering currant, early clematis and most rhododendrons. Cut them now and you cut off this year's flowers. Prune them straight after flowering instead.
  • Plums, cherries and apricots. Stone fruit is prone to silver leaf disease, which gets in through winter wounds. Prune in summer, when the cuts heal quickly.
  • Evergreens, apart from a light tidy. Any hard cutting can wait until late spring, when new growth will cover the cuts.
  • Anything you are not sure about. Leaving a plant unpruned for a year rarely harms it. Cutting the wrong thing at the wrong time often does.

A few habits worth having

Keep your secateurs sharp and clean. A crushed stem heals slowly and lets disease in. Wipe the blades between plants if you are cutting out anything that looks diseased.

Cut just above a bud, at a slight angle away from it, so water runs off. Do not leave long stubs; they die back and rot.

Step back often. It is very easy to get absorbed in one branch and lose sight of the shape of the whole plant. We stop every few cuts and look from a distance, and so should you.

The most useful pruning tool is a cup of tea and five minutes of looking before you start.

If you have an old or overgrown tree or shrub that needs more than a tidy, it is worth getting someone in to look at it. Restoring a neglected apple tree, for instance, is a job for three winters, not one afternoon.

values.title: Reworking a 1970s school playground in Gateshead
values.excerpt: How we turned a tarmac yard into somewhere to play, learn and calm down, with the help of the children who use it.
values.body:
Last summer we finished work on the playground of a primary school in Gateshead. The original was laid in the 1970s and was, in the words of the head teacher, "a car park without the cars". Tarmac from wall to wall, a painted hopscotch, and one tree in a cage.

The school wanted somewhere children could play, learn and calm down, on a budget raised mostly by the parents' association and a local grant. This post is about how we approached it, and what we learned.

Asking the children

We spent two mornings in the school before drawing anything. The children drew their ideal playground, walked us round the current one, and told us where they went when they wanted to be on their own. (Behind the bins, mostly.)

A few things came up again and again:

  • somewhere to hide that was not behind the bins;
  • something to climb that was not the fence;
  • a place to sit with friends out of the wind;
  • more trees, and things growing.

None of that needed expensive play equipment. All of it needed the space to be broken up.

What we built

We kept about half of the tarmac for running games and ball play, because children need open space and the school needed somewhere to line up. The other half we lifted and replaced with:

  1. A low mound, planted with native hedging and small trees, with a willow tunnel through the middle.
  2. Boulders and logs for climbing and sitting, set into bark.
  3. Six raised beds, one for each year group, at child height.
  4. A sheltered seating area under a timber canopy, facing away from the prevailing wind.

The caged tree was freed, and we planted eleven more.

A year on

The willow tunnel is now the most popular place in the school. The raised beds produced potatoes, beans and a remarkable number of sunflowers. The staff tell us that lunchtimes are noticeably calmer, and that fewer children come in with grazed knees, which we had not expected.

The quiet children have somewhere to be now. That was the thing I most wanted.

What we learned

School grounds take heavy wear. We used tougher plants than we would in a garden, protected new hedging with temporary fencing for the first year, and chose bark over grass in the busiest areas. We also wrote a simple maintenance plan that the school and parents can follow without us.

We would like to do more of this kind of work. If your school is thinking about its grounds, we would be glad to hear from you.

values.title: Welcome, Priya: our new planting designer
values.excerpt: Priya Raman joins Northfold from five years running trial beds at a North Yorkshire nursery.
values.body:
We are very pleased to say that Priya Raman has joined Northfold as our planting designer.

Priya comes to us from five years at a nursery in North Yorkshire, where she ran the trial beds and grew most of the perennials that went out to garden designers across the region. Before that she studied horticulture at Askham Bryan and spent two summers working on the borders at a large historic garden in Cumbria.

In other words, she knows plants from the root up, and has spent a long time watching which ones actually thrive in a northern garden rather than just looking good in a catalogue.

What she will be doing

Priya will lead the planting on most of our projects from now on. That means:

  • visiting sites at the start, alongside the rest of us, to look at soil, aspect and what already grows well;
  • drawing up the planting plans and plant lists;
  • sourcing plants, mostly from nurseries within a couple of hours of the studio;
  • setting out and overseeing the planting on site;
  • going back after the first year to see what has worked and adjust.

That last part matters a great deal to us. A planting plan is a best guess. The garden always has its own ideas, and someone needs to listen to them.

In her own words

I like plants that earn their space. If something only looks good for three weeks, it needs a very good reason to be there.

That sums up her approach well, and it fits ours. Expect more grasses, more plants that stand through winter, and fewer that need staking.

Meet her

Priya is in the studio most Tuesdays and Thursdays and on site the rest of the week. If you are a current client, you will meet her at your next site visit. If you are thinking about a project and would like to talk planting in particular, ask for her when you get in touch.

We are also planning a short series of posts from Priya on plants that do well in the North East, starting with the ones she would never be without. The first should be up next month.

Welcome, Priya. We are glad you are here.

values.title: Planting for winter structure
values.excerpt: A garden that looks good in January almost always looks good in July. So we plan for winter first.
values.body:
For about four months of the year, a garden in the north of England is mostly bones. The flowers have gone, the leaves have dropped, and what is left is the outline: hedges, trees, paths, walls and whatever plants hold their shape through the cold.

A garden that looks good in January almost always looks good in July. The reverse is not true. So when we plan planting, we start with winter.

Evergreens, used sparingly

Evergreens give a garden its year-round frame, but too many make it feel heavy and static. We tend to aim for about a third of the planting being evergreen, placed where it does a job:

  • Clipped yew or box-leaved holly at corners and entrances, to mark where things begin and end.
  • A loose evergreen hedge along a boundary you would rather not look at.
  • One or two larger shrubs, such as osmanthus or phillyrea, as backdrops to plants that are bare in winter.

Bark and stems

Some of the best winter colour is on plants with no leaves at all. Red and yellow dogwoods cut hard each spring give bright stems the following winter. Birch, especially the white-barked forms, catches low light beautifully. Paperbark maple and the Tibetan cherry are worth growing for their bark alone.

Place them where the winter sun will reach them in the afternoon, and where you will see them from the house.

Plants that die well

This is the part people often overlook. Many perennials and grasses look as good dead as alive, provided you leave them standing.

  1. Grasses such as miscanthus, molinia and calamagrostis stand up to wind and rain and turn the colour of straw.
  2. Seedheads of echinacea, phlomis, eryngium and sedum hold frost and snow in a way that photographs well and feeds birds.
  3. Tall umbellifers like fennel and angelica leave skeletons that last until March.

The hard landscape

In winter, paths, walls and steps carry much more of the design. If a path does not lead anywhere, you notice it. If a bench is in the wrong place, it looks lost. We often draw the garden as if it had no plants at all, just to check the structure works on its own.

Plan for January, and July tends to look after itself.

If your garden feels empty for half the year, it usually needs a few well-placed shrubs and some patience with the secateurs in autumn, rather than more flowers.

values.title: The Calder Street courtyard: shade, brick and ferns
values.excerpt: A small courtyard with three hours of summer sun, planted as a woodland floor rather than a sunny terrace.
values.body:
The courtyard behind the house on Calder Street gets about three hours of direct sun in midsummer and none at all from November to February. It is enclosed on three sides by brick, two storeys high, and the fourth side is the kitchen.

When the owners first called us, they described it as a cupboard. They had tried pots of lavender and a small olive tree, and both had given up within a season.

Working with the shade

The first decision was to stop fighting it. Shade is not a problem to be solved in a space like this. It is the character of the place, and some of the best plants we know want exactly these conditions.

So we planted for a woodland floor, not a sunny terrace:

  • Ferns, in quantity. Hart's tongue along the base of the walls, soft shield fern in the corners, and a single tree fern by the kitchen window, where it can be seen from the sink.
  • Hellebores and epimediums for winter and early spring, when the courtyard most needs something to look at.
  • Japanese anemones and hydrangeas for late summer, in white, which glows in low light.
  • A multi-stemmed amelanchier as the one tree. It is light enough not to darken the space further, and it flowers, fruits and colours in autumn.

The brick

The walls were the courtyard's best asset and had been painted cream at some point. We had the paint taken off, which took longer than anything else on the job, and repointed where it needed it. Old brick holds warmth and moss, and against it the green of the ferns looks deeper.

For the floor we used reclaimed setts, laid with wide joints so that moss and a few small ferns can find their way in. It will look better every year.

Light at night

Because the courtyard is mostly seen from the kitchen, we spent time on the lighting. Two low lights wash up the back wall, and one picks out the tree fern from below. In winter, when the garden is dark by four, it gives the kitchen a view rather than a black window.

It doesn't feel like a cupboard any more. It feels like somewhere we chose.

Looking after it

A shady courtyard is easy to maintain if it is planted well. There is no lawn and very little to deadhead. The main jobs are cutting back old fern fronds in March, mulching with leaf mould in autumn, and keeping an eye on watering in the first summer, since walls cast a rain shadow as well as a sun one.

We left the owners with a one-page calendar of what to do and when. It fits on the fridge, which is where, we are told, it lives.

values.title: Rain gardens for ordinary front gardens
values.excerpt: A planted hollow that catches water from a roof and lets it sink in slowly. Simpler than it sounds, and it works in more places than you would think.
values.body:
Most front gardens in the North East were paved at some point in the last thirty years, usually to park a car. It made sense at the time. The trouble is that all the rain that used to soak into that soil now runs straight into the drains, and in a heavy storm the drains cannot cope.

A rain garden is one small way to put some of that back. It sounds technical, but it is really just a planted dip that catches water from a roof or a path and lets it sink in slowly.

How it works

You disconnect a downpipe, or part of one, and send the water across the surface into a shallow planted hollow. The hollow fills in a downpour and drains within a day or two. The plants are chosen to cope with both: wet feet for a while, then dry spells in summer.

The aim is not to hold water permanently. If it is still standing after forty-eight hours, the soil needs opening up or the hollow needs to be bigger.

Will it work in my garden?

It works in more places than people expect. A few things to check first:

  • It should sit at least a few metres from the house, so water is not sent towards the foundations.
  • Very heavy clay drains slowly. You can still do it, but the hollow needs to be wider and shallower, with grit dug into the base.
  • Do not build one over a septic tank, a soakaway or a cellar.

A simple test: dig a hole about thirty centimetres deep, fill it with water, and see how long it takes to empty. Under a day is ideal. Two days is workable.

What to plant

We use a mix of plants that cope with both wet and dry, and keep the wettest-loving ones in the bottom of the dip.

  • In the base: purple loosestrife, meadowsweet, the smaller sedges and flag iris if there is room.
  • On the slopes: hardy geraniums, astrantia, sanguisorba and some of the taller grasses.
  • Around the rim: anything that suits the rest of the garden, as this part stays relatively dry.

Is it worth it?

One rain garden will not stop a street from flooding. But it does take a real share of the water off a single roof, it looks far better than a gully, and it brings insects and birds into a part of the garden that usually has none.

We have built several now, from a small one beside a terraced house in Heaton to a long swale along a school drive. If you are thinking about one, we are happy to come and have a look.

values.title: Why we start every project with a site walk
values.excerpt: Before any drawings, we spend two hours walking the garden with the people who use it. Here is why.
values.body:
Every Northfold project starts the same way. Before any drawings, before any talk of budgets or planting lists, we walk the site with the people who use it. It usually takes about two hours. It is the most useful two hours of the whole job.

What we are looking for

Some of it is technical. We look at the soil, the drainage, where the water goes after rain, which way the wind comes from and where the frost sits. We note every tree, every level change and every view worth keeping or hiding.

But most of it is about people. Where do you stand when you come out of the back door? Where does the sun reach at six in the evening in June? Where do the children actually play, as opposed to where the lawn is? Which corner do you avoid?

These things are hard to describe in an email and easy to see on the ground.

Why it saves money

A garden designed from a plan and a few photographs can look right on paper and work badly. The bench ends up in the shade. The path takes the long way round. The planting that suited the drawing does not suit the soil.

Fixing those things after a garden is built is expensive. Spotting them on a walk costs nothing.

We would rather ask a hundred small questions at the start than one big one at the end.

What happens next

After the walk we write a short summary of what we saw and heard, with a few early ideas and an honest view of what the budget will and will not cover. There is no obligation at that point. Some people take the summary and do the work themselves, and we are glad when they do.

If you would like us to carry on, the next stage is a measured survey and a concept plan. We will tell you what that costs before we start.

What to have ready

You do not need to prepare anything, but a few things help:

  1. A rough idea of what you want the garden for, even if it is just a list of complaints about how it is now.
  2. Any old plans, deeds or surveys you have, especially if they show drains or boundaries.
  3. Everyone who will use the garden, if you can manage it. The person who mows the lawn often sees it very differently from the person who chose the plants.

Then put the kettle on. The best ideas usually come up somewhere around the second cup.

values.title: What to do in the garden in October
values.excerpt: The soil is still warm and the light is dropping. A short list of what is worth doing this month, and what can wait.
values.body:
October is the month when the garden starts to tell you what it wants for next year. The light drops, the soil is still warm, and there is a short window where planting does more good than at almost any other time.

Here is what we are doing in our own gardens, and what we suggest to clients who ask.

Plant now, not in spring

Trees, shrubs and most perennials go in better now than in April. The roots have weeks of warm soil to settle into before winter, and they start the spring already established. A shrub planted in October will usually need half the watering of one planted at Easter.

Bare-root hedging arrives from November, so this is the month to prepare the ground for it. Dig the trench, add some well-rotted compost, and leave it to settle.

Leave the seedheads

It is tempting to cut everything back and tidy up. We would ask you not to, or at least not all of it.

  • Grasses, sedums and the tall daisies hold their shape through frost and look wonderful in low sun.
  • Seedheads feed finches and give insects somewhere to spend the winter.
  • Hollow stems are where solitary bees overwinter. Cut them in spring, at different heights, and leave the stubs.

Cut back anything that has collapsed or gone to mush, and leave the rest until February.

Lift and divide

Clumps that have gone bare in the middle, such as hardy geraniums, asters and most grasses that grow in the warm, can be lifted now and split. Use two forks back to back if they are stubborn. Replant the young outer pieces and compost the woody centre.

Look after the soil

Once the borders are mostly bare, a layer of mulch does more for next year than anything else you can do this month. We go into this at length in another post, but the short version is: five centimetres of compost or leaf mould, on damp soil, before the first hard frost.

Write it down

The last job is the one most people skip. Walk round with a notebook and write down what worked, what sulked, and what you never got round to. In March you will have forgotten, and the notes will make the spring much easier.

If you would like help planning next year, we are taking on a few new projects for the spring. Get in touch and we will arrange a site walk.

values.title: A walled garden in Hexham, two years on
values.excerpt: We went back to a walled kitchen garden we redesigned two years ago, to see how it has settled and what we would change.
values.body:
Two years ago we were asked to look at a walled kitchen garden on the edge of Hexham. The walls were sound, the soil was tired, and the owners had inherited a layout that nobody could quite explain. Paths stopped short of anything useful. A greenhouse faced north. There was a pond where the best light fell.

We went back last month to see how it has settled in, and it seemed a good moment to write down what we did and what we would do differently.

What the garden needed

The brief was short. The family wanted to grow vegetables again, to sit somewhere warm in the evening, and to stop losing a weekend every spring to weeding gravel. They did not want it to look new.

So we kept the walls, the old pear trained against the south side, and most of the brick edging, which we lifted, cleaned and relaid. Everything else was up for discussion.

What we changed

  • The paths. We redrew them on the lines people actually walked, which we found by asking the family to spend a week noting where they cut across the beds. Two paths became one wide one, in bound gravel that does not need raking.
  • The beds. Four raised beds in oak, at a height that suits the grandparents as well as the children. They are narrow enough to reach the middle without stepping on the soil.
  • The pond. We filled it in and moved the water to a stone trough by the door, where it catches the morning sun and the birds use it daily.
  • The greenhouse. Rebuilt against the north wall so the glass faces south. The same frame, mostly; new glazing and a brick base from the old path.

Two years on

The planting along the walls has filled in more quickly than we expected. The espaliered apples we added are already cropping, and the herb border under the pear has seeded itself into the gravel edges in a way that looks as though it has always been there. That was the hope.

We spend more time in it now than we did in the house last summer.

That is from the owners, and it is the best thing anyone has said about our work this year.

What we would do differently

The oak beds are lovely, but we specified them a little too tall. Fifteen centimetres lower would have been easier for planting out and would have dried out less in July. We have noted it for the next one.

We would also have left more room by the gate. Barrows, bikes and bags of compost all arrive at the same place, and it is tighter than it should be.

Neither is a big problem. Both are the kind of thing you only learn by going back, which is why we always do.

values.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
values.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
values.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

What it does

  • It keeps moisture in. A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
  • It suppresses weeds. Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
  • It feeds the soil. Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
  • It protects roots from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
  • It makes a border look finished, which matters more than people admit.

When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

  1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
  2. Water if the soil is dry.
  3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
  4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

values.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
values.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
values.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

  • The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
  • The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
  • The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

How it has settled

Three summers on, the meadow is starting to find its balance. The first year was mostly annual cornfield flowers, as it always is. Since then the perennials have taken over: knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, field scabious and a good deal of yellow rattle, which keeps the grass in check.

We walk down to the bottom most evenings now. We never used to go past the washing line.

Slopes put many people off, but they make some of the most rewarding gardens to design. The changes in level give you views, shelter and a sense of journey that a flat plot cannot.

values.title: We've moved: the new studio on Wharf Lane
values.excerpt: After six years above a bike shop, Northfold now works from a converted joinery workshop by the river.
values.body:
After six years in two rooms above a bike shop, Northfold has a new home. Since the start of the month we have been working from a converted joinery workshop on Wharf Lane, a few minutes' walk from the river.

It is a big change for a small studio, and we wanted to say a little about why we moved and what the new space means for the work.

Why we moved

Honestly, we ran out of room. When there were three of us, two rooms were plenty. Now there are six, plus a growing library of samples, a plan chest, two bicycles and more plants on the windowsills than any landlord would like.

We also wanted somewhere clients could visit. Most of our first meetings happen on site, which is how we like it, but there comes a point in every project where it helps to sit round a big table with the drawings, the samples and the planting lists all out at once. The old studio simply could not do that.

The new space

The workshop dates from the 1890s and was used by a joinery firm until about ten years ago. It has a high timber roof, a long run of north-facing windows that give steady, even light all day, and a yard at the back.

Inside we have:

  • a large shared studio with room for everyone and a little to spare;
  • a meeting room with a table big enough for a full set of plans;
  • a materials wall, with samples of the stone, brick, gravel and timber we use most;
  • a small kitchen, which is already the busiest room in the building.

The yard

The yard is the part we are most excited about. At the moment it is concrete and nettles. Over the next year we are going to turn it into a working garden: a place to trial plants before we use them on projects, test paving and gravel through a northern winter, and grow cut flowers for the studio.

We will share how it goes, including the parts that do not work.

Come and see us

We are planning a small open afternoon in the spring, once the yard has something growing in it. Clients, past and present, neighbours and anyone curious will be welcome. We will post the date here nearer the time.

In the meantime, if you are passing and the door is open, do come in. The kettle is usually on.

values.title: Pruning in late winter: what to cut and what to leave
values.excerpt: Late winter is pruning season for a good share of the garden. How we decide what to cut now, and what to leave alone.
values.body:
Late winter is pruning season for a good share of the garden. The sap is not yet rising, the shape of each plant is easy to see, and there is not much else to do outside. But it is also when the most damage gets done with secateurs, usually with the best intentions.

Here is how we decide what to cut now, and what to leave alone.

Cut now

  • Late-flowering clematis (the ones that flower from midsummer on). Cut every stem back to a pair of fat buds about thirty centimetres above the ground. It feels brutal. They love it.
  • Buddleja, lavatera and hardy fuchsias. These flower on new growth, so a hard cut now gives you more flowers later.
  • Dogwoods and willows grown for their stems. Cut all or a third of the stems to the base, depending on how much colour you want next winter.
  • Apples and pears, if they are free-standing. Take out dead, crossing and inward-facing branches and aim for an open, goblet shape.
  • Wisteria, for its second prune of the year. Shorten the side shoots you cut back in summer to two or three buds.

Leave alone

  • Anything that flowers in spring, such as forsythia, flowering currant, early clematis and most rhododendrons. Cut them now and you cut off this year's flowers. Prune them straight after flowering instead.
  • Plums, cherries and apricots. Stone fruit is prone to silver leaf disease, which gets in through winter wounds. Prune in summer, when the cuts heal quickly.
  • Evergreens, apart from a light tidy. Any hard cutting can wait until late spring, when new growth will cover the cuts.
  • Anything you are not sure about. Leaving a plant unpruned for a year rarely harms it. Cutting the wrong thing at the wrong time often does.

A few habits worth having

Keep your secateurs sharp and clean. A crushed stem heals slowly and lets disease in. Wipe the blades between plants if you are cutting out anything that looks diseased.

Cut just above a bud, at a slight angle away from it, so water runs off. Do not leave long stubs; they die back and rot.

Step back often. It is very easy to get absorbed in one branch and lose sight of the shape of the whole plant. We stop every few cuts and look from a distance, and so should you.

The most useful pruning tool is a cup of tea and five minutes of looking before you start.

If you have an old or overgrown tree or shrub that needs more than a tidy, it is worth getting someone in to look at it. Restoring a neglected apple tree, for instance, is a job for three winters, not one afternoon.

values.title: Reworking a 1970s school playground in Gateshead
values.excerpt: How we turned a tarmac yard into somewhere to play, learn and calm down, with the help of the children who use it.
values.body:
Last summer we finished work on the playground of a primary school in Gateshead. The original was laid in the 1970s and was, in the words of the head teacher, "a car park without the cars". Tarmac from wall to wall, a painted hopscotch, and one tree in a cage.

The school wanted somewhere children could play, learn and calm down, on a budget raised mostly by the parents' association and a local grant. This post is about how we approached it, and what we learned.

Asking the children

We spent two mornings in the school before drawing anything. The children drew their ideal playground, walked us round the current one, and told us where they went when they wanted to be on their own. (Behind the bins, mostly.)

A few things came up again and again:

  • somewhere to hide that was not behind the bins;
  • something to climb that was not the fence;
  • a place to sit with friends out of the wind;
  • more trees, and things growing.

None of that needed expensive play equipment. All of it needed the space to be broken up.

What we built

We kept about half of the tarmac for running games and ball play, because children need open space and the school needed somewhere to line up. The other half we lifted and replaced with:

  1. A low mound, planted with native hedging and small trees, with a willow tunnel through the middle.
  2. Boulders and logs for climbing and sitting, set into bark.
  3. Six raised beds, one for each year group, at child height.
  4. A sheltered seating area under a timber canopy, facing away from the prevailing wind.

The caged tree was freed, and we planted eleven more.

A year on

The willow tunnel is now the most popular place in the school. The raised beds produced potatoes, beans and a remarkable number of sunflowers. The staff tell us that lunchtimes are noticeably calmer, and that fewer children come in with grazed knees, which we had not expected.

The quiet children have somewhere to be now. That was the thing I most wanted.

What we learned

School grounds take heavy wear. We used tougher plants than we would in a garden, protected new hedging with temporary fencing for the first year, and chose bark over grass in the busiest areas. We also wrote a simple maintenance plan that the school and parents can follow without us.

We would like to do more of this kind of work. If your school is thinking about its grounds, we would be glad to hear from you.

values.title: Welcome, Priya: our new planting designer
values.excerpt: Priya Raman joins Northfold from five years running trial beds at a North Yorkshire nursery.
values.body:
We are very pleased to say that Priya Raman has joined Northfold as our planting designer.

Priya comes to us from five years at a nursery in North Yorkshire, where she ran the trial beds and grew most of the perennials that went out to garden designers across the region. Before that she studied horticulture at Askham Bryan and spent two summers working on the borders at a large historic garden in Cumbria.

In other words, she knows plants from the root up, and has spent a long time watching which ones actually thrive in a northern garden rather than just looking good in a catalogue.

What she will be doing

Priya will lead the planting on most of our projects from now on. That means:

  • visiting sites at the start, alongside the rest of us, to look at soil, aspect and what already grows well;
  • drawing up the planting plans and plant lists;
  • sourcing plants, mostly from nurseries within a couple of hours of the studio;
  • setting out and overseeing the planting on site;
  • going back after the first year to see what has worked and adjust.

That last part matters a great deal to us. A planting plan is a best guess. The garden always has its own ideas, and someone needs to listen to them.

In her own words

I like plants that earn their space. If something only looks good for three weeks, it needs a very good reason to be there.

That sums up her approach well, and it fits ours. Expect more grasses, more plants that stand through winter, and fewer that need staking.

Meet her

Priya is in the studio most Tuesdays and Thursdays and on site the rest of the week. If you are a current client, you will meet her at your next site visit. If you are thinking about a project and would like to talk planting in particular, ask for her when you get in touch.

We are also planning a short series of posts from Priya on plants that do well in the North East, starting with the ones she would never be without. The first should be up next month.

Welcome, Priya. We are glad you are here.

values.title: Planting for winter structure
values.excerpt: A garden that looks good in January almost always looks good in July. So we plan for winter first.
values.body:
For about four months of the year, a garden in the north of England is mostly bones. The flowers have gone, the leaves have dropped, and what is left is the outline: hedges, trees, paths, walls and whatever plants hold their shape through the cold.

A garden that looks good in January almost always looks good in July. The reverse is not true. So when we plan planting, we start with winter.

Evergreens, used sparingly

Evergreens give a garden its year-round frame, but too many make it feel heavy and static. We tend to aim for about a third of the planting being evergreen, placed where it does a job:

  • Clipped yew or box-leaved holly at corners and entrances, to mark where things begin and end.
  • A loose evergreen hedge along a boundary you would rather not look at.
  • One or two larger shrubs, such as osmanthus or phillyrea, as backdrops to plants that are bare in winter.

Bark and stems

Some of the best winter colour is on plants with no leaves at all. Red and yellow dogwoods cut hard each spring give bright stems the following winter. Birch, especially the white-barked forms, catches low light beautifully. Paperbark maple and the Tibetan cherry are worth growing for their bark alone.

Place them where the winter sun will reach them in the afternoon, and where you will see them from the house.

Plants that die well

This is the part people often overlook. Many perennials and grasses look as good dead as alive, provided you leave them standing.

  1. Grasses such as miscanthus, molinia and calamagrostis stand up to wind and rain and turn the colour of straw.
  2. Seedheads of echinacea, phlomis, eryngium and sedum hold frost and snow in a way that photographs well and feeds birds.
  3. Tall umbellifers like fennel and angelica leave skeletons that last until March.

The hard landscape

In winter, paths, walls and steps carry much more of the design. If a path does not lead anywhere, you notice it. If a bench is in the wrong place, it looks lost. We often draw the garden as if it had no plants at all, just to check the structure works on its own.

Plan for January, and July tends to look after itself.

If your garden feels empty for half the year, it usually needs a few well-placed shrubs and some patience with the secateurs in autumn, rather than more flowers.

values.title: The Calder Street courtyard: shade, brick and ferns
values.excerpt: A small courtyard with three hours of summer sun, planted as a woodland floor rather than a sunny terrace.
values.body:
The courtyard behind the house on Calder Street gets about three hours of direct sun in midsummer and none at all from November to February. It is enclosed on three sides by brick, two storeys high, and the fourth side is the kitchen.

When the owners first called us, they described it as a cupboard. They had tried pots of lavender and a small olive tree, and both had given up within a season.

Working with the shade

The first decision was to stop fighting it. Shade is not a problem to be solved in a space like this. It is the character of the place, and some of the best plants we know want exactly these conditions.

So we planted for a woodland floor, not a sunny terrace:

  • Ferns, in quantity. Hart's tongue along the base of the walls, soft shield fern in the corners, and a single tree fern by the kitchen window, where it can be seen from the sink.
  • Hellebores and epimediums for winter and early spring, when the courtyard most needs something to look at.
  • Japanese anemones and hydrangeas for late summer, in white, which glows in low light.
  • A multi-stemmed amelanchier as the one tree. It is light enough not to darken the space further, and it flowers, fruits and colours in autumn.

The brick

The walls were the courtyard's best asset and had been painted cream at some point. We had the paint taken off, which took longer than anything else on the job, and repointed where it needed it. Old brick holds warmth and moss, and against it the green of the ferns looks deeper.

For the floor we used reclaimed setts, laid with wide joints so that moss and a few small ferns can find their way in. It will look better every year.

Light at night

Because the courtyard is mostly seen from the kitchen, we spent time on the lighting. Two low lights wash up the back wall, and one picks out the tree fern from below. In winter, when the garden is dark by four, it gives the kitchen a view rather than a black window.

It doesn't feel like a cupboard any more. It feels like somewhere we chose.

Looking after it

A shady courtyard is easy to maintain if it is planted well. There is no lawn and very little to deadhead. The main jobs are cutting back old fern fronds in March, mulching with leaf mould in autumn, and keeping an eye on watering in the first summer, since walls cast a rain shadow as well as a sun one.

We left the owners with a one-page calendar of what to do and when. It fits on the fridge, which is where, we are told, it lives.

values.title: Rain gardens for ordinary front gardens
values.excerpt: A planted hollow that catches water from a roof and lets it sink in slowly. Simpler than it sounds, and it works in more places than you would think.
values.body:
Most front gardens in the North East were paved at some point in the last thirty years, usually to park a car. It made sense at the time. The trouble is that all the rain that used to soak into that soil now runs straight into the drains, and in a heavy storm the drains cannot cope.

A rain garden is one small way to put some of that back. It sounds technical, but it is really just a planted dip that catches water from a roof or a path and lets it sink in slowly.

How it works

You disconnect a downpipe, or part of one, and send the water across the surface into a shallow planted hollow. The hollow fills in a downpour and drains within a day or two. The plants are chosen to cope with both: wet feet for a while, then dry spells in summer.

The aim is not to hold water permanently. If it is still standing after forty-eight hours, the soil needs opening up or the hollow needs to be bigger.

Will it work in my garden?

It works in more places than people expect. A few things to check first:

  • It should sit at least a few metres from the house, so water is not sent towards the foundations.
  • Very heavy clay drains slowly. You can still do it, but the hollow needs to be wider and shallower, with grit dug into the base.
  • Do not build one over a septic tank, a soakaway or a cellar.

A simple test: dig a hole about thirty centimetres deep, fill it with water, and see how long it takes to empty. Under a day is ideal. Two days is workable.

What to plant

We use a mix of plants that cope with both wet and dry, and keep the wettest-loving ones in the bottom of the dip.

  • In the base: purple loosestrife, meadowsweet, the smaller sedges and flag iris if there is room.
  • On the slopes: hardy geraniums, astrantia, sanguisorba and some of the taller grasses.
  • Around the rim: anything that suits the rest of the garden, as this part stays relatively dry.

Is it worth it?

One rain garden will not stop a street from flooding. But it does take a real share of the water off a single roof, it looks far better than a gully, and it brings insects and birds into a part of the garden that usually has none.

We have built several now, from a small one beside a terraced house in Heaton to a long swale along a school drive. If you are thinking about one, we are happy to come and have a look.

values.title: Why we start every project with a site walk
values.excerpt: Before any drawings, we spend two hours walking the garden with the people who use it. Here is why.
values.body:
Every Northfold project starts the same way. Before any drawings, before any talk of budgets or planting lists, we walk the site with the people who use it. It usually takes about two hours. It is the most useful two hours of the whole job.

What we are looking for

Some of it is technical. We look at the soil, the drainage, where the water goes after rain, which way the wind comes from and where the frost sits. We note every tree, every level change and every view worth keeping or hiding.

But most of it is about people. Where do you stand when you come out of the back door? Where does the sun reach at six in the evening in June? Where do the children actually play, as opposed to where the lawn is? Which corner do you avoid?

These things are hard to describe in an email and easy to see on the ground.

Why it saves money

A garden designed from a plan and a few photographs can look right on paper and work badly. The bench ends up in the shade. The path takes the long way round. The planting that suited the drawing does not suit the soil.

Fixing those things after a garden is built is expensive. Spotting them on a walk costs nothing.

We would rather ask a hundred small questions at the start than one big one at the end.

What happens next

After the walk we write a short summary of what we saw and heard, with a few early ideas and an honest view of what the budget will and will not cover. There is no obligation at that point. Some people take the summary and do the work themselves, and we are glad when they do.

If you would like us to carry on, the next stage is a measured survey and a concept plan. We will tell you what that costs before we start.

What to have ready

You do not need to prepare anything, but a few things help:

  1. A rough idea of what you want the garden for, even if it is just a list of complaints about how it is now.
  2. Any old plans, deeds or surveys you have, especially if they show drains or boundaries.
  3. Everyone who will use the garden, if you can manage it. The person who mows the lawn often sees it very differently from the person who chose the plants.

Then put the kettle on. The best ideas usually come up somewhere around the second cup.

values.title: What to do in the garden in October
values.excerpt: The soil is still warm and the light is dropping. A short list of what is worth doing this month, and what can wait.
values.body:
October is the month when the garden starts to tell you what it wants for next year. The light drops, the soil is still warm, and there is a short window where planting does more good than at almost any other time.

Here is what we are doing in our own gardens, and what we suggest to clients who ask.

Plant now, not in spring

Trees, shrubs and most perennials go in better now than in April. The roots have weeks of warm soil to settle into before winter, and they start the spring already established. A shrub planted in October will usually need half the watering of one planted at Easter.

Bare-root hedging arrives from November, so this is the month to prepare the ground for it. Dig the trench, add some well-rotted compost, and leave it to settle.

Leave the seedheads

It is tempting to cut everything back and tidy up. We would ask you not to, or at least not all of it.

  • Grasses, sedums and the tall daisies hold their shape through frost and look wonderful in low sun.
  • Seedheads feed finches and give insects somewhere to spend the winter.
  • Hollow stems are where solitary bees overwinter. Cut them in spring, at different heights, and leave the stubs.

Cut back anything that has collapsed or gone to mush, and leave the rest until February.

Lift and divide

Clumps that have gone bare in the middle, such as hardy geraniums, asters and most grasses that grow in the warm, can be lifted now and split. Use two forks back to back if they are stubborn. Replant the young outer pieces and compost the woody centre.

Look after the soil

Once the borders are mostly bare, a layer of mulch does more for next year than anything else you can do this month. We go into this at length in another post, but the short version is: five centimetres of compost or leaf mould, on damp soil, before the first hard frost.

Write it down

The last job is the one most people skip. Walk round with a notebook and write down what worked, what sulked, and what you never got round to. In March you will have forgotten, and the notes will make the spring much easier.

If you would like help planning next year, we are taking on a few new projects for the spring. Get in touch and we will arrange a site walk.

values.title: A walled garden in Hexham, two years on
values.excerpt: We went back to a walled kitchen garden we redesigned two years ago, to see how it has settled and what we would change.
values.body:
Two years ago we were asked to look at a walled kitchen garden on the edge of Hexham. The walls were sound, the soil was tired, and the owners had inherited a layout that nobody could quite explain. Paths stopped short of anything useful. A greenhouse faced north. There was a pond where the best light fell.

We went back last month to see how it has settled in, and it seemed a good moment to write down what we did and what we would do differently.

What the garden needed

The brief was short. The family wanted to grow vegetables again, to sit somewhere warm in the evening, and to stop losing a weekend every spring to weeding gravel. They did not want it to look new.

So we kept the walls, the old pear trained against the south side, and most of the brick edging, which we lifted, cleaned and relaid. Everything else was up for discussion.

What we changed

  • The paths. We redrew them on the lines people actually walked, which we found by asking the family to spend a week noting where they cut across the beds. Two paths became one wide one, in bound gravel that does not need raking.
  • The beds. Four raised beds in oak, at a height that suits the grandparents as well as the children. They are narrow enough to reach the middle without stepping on the soil.
  • The pond. We filled it in and moved the water to a stone trough by the door, where it catches the morning sun and the birds use it daily.
  • The greenhouse. Rebuilt against the north wall so the glass faces south. The same frame, mostly; new glazing and a brick base from the old path.

Two years on

The planting along the walls has filled in more quickly than we expected. The espaliered apples we added are already cropping, and the herb border under the pear has seeded itself into the gravel edges in a way that looks as though it has always been there. That was the hope.

We spend more time in it now than we did in the house last summer.

That is from the owners, and it is the best thing anyone has said about our work this year.

What we would do differently

The oak beds are lovely, but we specified them a little too tall. Fifteen centimetres lower would have been easier for planting out and would have dried out less in July. We have noted it for the next one.

We would also have left more room by the gate. Barrows, bikes and bags of compost all arrive at the same place, and it is tighter than it should be.

Neither is a big problem. Both are the kind of thing you only learn by going back, which is why we always do.

examples.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
examples.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
examples.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

## What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

## What it does

- **It keeps moisture in.** A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
- **It suppresses weeds.** Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
- **It feeds the soil.** Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
- **It protects roots** from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
- **It makes a border look finished** , which matters more than people admit.

## When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
2. Water if the soil is dry.
3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

## Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

> Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

examples.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
examples.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.

examples.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
examples.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
examples.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

## Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

## A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

## Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

- The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
- The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
- The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

## How it has settled

Three summers on, the meadow is starting to find its balance. The first year was mostly annual cornfield flowers, as it always is. Since then the perennials have taken over: knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, field scabious and a good deal of yellow rattle, which keeps the grass in check.

> We walk down to the bottom most evenings now. We never used to go past the washing line.

Slopes put many people off, but they make some of the most rewarding gardens to design. The changes in level give you views, shelter and a sense of journey that a flat plot cannot.

After six years in two rooms above a bike shop, Northfold has a new home. Since the start of the month we have been working from a converted joinery workshop on Wharf Lane, a few minutes' walk from the river.

It is a big change for a small studio, and we wanted to say a little about why we moved and what the new space means for the work.

## Why we moved

Honestly, we ran out of room. When there were three of us, two rooms were plenty. Now there are six, plus a growing library of samples, a plan chest, two bicycles and more plants on the windowsills than any landlord would like.

We also wanted somewhere clients could visit. Most of our first meetings happen on site, which is how we like it, but there comes a point in every project where it helps to sit round a big table with the drawings, the samples and the planting lists all out at once. The old studio simply could not do that.

## The new space

The workshop dates from the 1890s and was used by a joinery firm until about ten years ago. It has a high timber roof, a long run of north-facing windows that give steady, even light all day, and a yard at the back.

Inside we have:

- a large shared studio with room for everyone and a little to spare;
- a meeting room with a table big enough for a full set of plans;
- a materials wall, with samples of the stone, brick, gravel and timber we use most;
- a small kitchen, which is already the busiest room in the building.

## The yard

The yard is the part we are most excited about. At the moment it is concrete and nettles. Over the next year we are going to turn it into a working garden: a place to trial plants before we use them on projects, test paving and gravel through a northern winter, and grow cut flowers for the studio.

We will share how it goes, including the parts that do not work.

## Come and see us

We are planning a small open afternoon in the spring, once the yard has something growing in it. Clients, past and present, neighbours and anyone curious will be welcome. We will post the date here nearer the time.

In the meantime, if you are passing and the door is open, do come in. The kettle is usually on.

draft.title: Pruning in late winter: what to cut and what to leave
draft.excerpt: Late winter is pruning season for a good share of the garden. How we decide what to cut now, and what to leave alone.
draft.body:
Late winter is pruning season for a good share of the garden. The sap is not yet rising, the shape of each plant is easy to see, and there is not much else to do outside. But it is also when the most damage gets done with secateurs, usually with the best intentions.

Here is how we decide what to cut now, and what to leave alone.

## Cut now

- **Late-flowering clematis** (the ones that flower from midsummer on). Cut every stem back to a pair of fat buds about thirty centimetres above the ground. It feels brutal. They love it.
- **Buddleja, lavatera and hardy fuchsias.** These flower on new growth, so a hard cut now gives you more flowers later.
- **Dogwoods and willows grown for their stems.** Cut all or a third of the stems to the base, depending on how much colour you want next winter.
- **Apples and pears** , if they are free-standing. Take out dead, crossing and inward-facing branches and aim for an open, goblet shape.
- **Wisteria** , for its second prune of the year. Shorten the side shoots you cut back in summer to two or three buds.

## Leave alone

- **Anything that flowers in spring** , such as forsythia, flowering currant, early clematis and most rhododendrons. Cut them now and you cut off this year's flowers. Prune them straight after flowering instead.
- **Plums, cherries and apricots.** Stone fruit is prone to silver leaf disease, which gets in through winter wounds. Prune in summer, when the cuts heal quickly.
- **Evergreens** , apart from a light tidy. Any hard cutting can wait until late spring, when new growth will cover the cuts.
- **Anything you are not sure about.** Leaving a plant unpruned for a year rarely harms it. Cutting the wrong thing at the wrong time often does.

Keep your secateurs sharp and clean. A crushed stem heals slowly and lets disease in. Wipe the blades between plants if you are cutting out anything that looks diseased.

Cut just above a bud, at a slight angle away from it, so water runs off. Do not leave long stubs; they die back and rot.

Step back often. It is very easy to get absorbed in one branch and lose sight of the shape of the whole plant. We stop every few cuts and look from a distance, and so should you.

> The most useful pruning tool is a cup of tea and five minutes of looking before you start.

If you have an old or overgrown tree or shrub that needs more than a tidy, it is worth getting someone in to look at it. Restoring a neglected apple tree, for instance, is a job for three winters, not one afternoon.

examples.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
examples.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
examples.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

## What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

## What it does

- **It keeps moisture in.** A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
- **It suppresses weeds.** Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
- **It feeds the soil.** Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
- **It protects roots** from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
- **It makes a border look finished** , which matters more than people admit.

## When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
2. Water if the soil is dry.
3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

## Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

> Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

examples.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
examples.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
examples.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

## Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

## A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

## Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

- The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
- The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
- The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

## How it has settled

Three summers on, the meadow is starting to find its balance. The first year was mostly annual cornfield flowers, as it always is. Since then the perennials have taken over: knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, field scabious and a good deal of yellow rattle, which keeps the grass in check.

> We walk down to the bottom most evenings now. We never used to go past the washing line.

Slopes put many people off, but they make some of the most rewarding gardens to design. The changes in level give you views, shelter and a sense of journey that a flat plot cannot.

draft.title: Reworking a 1970s school playground in Gateshead
draft.excerpt: How we turned a tarmac yard into somewhere to play, learn and calm down, with the help of the children who use it.
draft.body:
Last summer we finished work on the playground of a primary school in Gateshead. The original was laid in the 1970s and was, in the words of the head teacher, "a car park without the cars". Tarmac from wall to wall, a painted hopscotch, and one tree in a cage.

The school wanted somewhere children could play, learn and calm down, on a budget raised mostly by the parents' association and a local grant. This post is about how we approached it, and what we learned.

## Asking the children

We spent two mornings in the school before drawing anything. The children drew their ideal playground, walked us round the current one, and told us where they went when they wanted to be on their own. (Behind the bins, mostly.)

A few things came up again and again:

- somewhere to hide that was not behind the bins;
- something to climb that was not the fence;
- a place to sit with friends out of the wind;
- more trees, and things growing.

None of that needed expensive play equipment. All of it needed the space to be broken up.

## What we built

We kept about half of the tarmac for running games and ball play, because children need open space and the school needed somewhere to line up. The other half we lifted and replaced with:

1. A low mound, planted with native hedging and small trees, with a willow tunnel through the middle.
2. Boulders and logs for climbing and sitting, set into bark.
3. Six raised beds, one for each year group, at child height.
4. A sheltered seating area under a timber canopy, facing away from the prevailing wind.

The caged tree was freed, and we planted eleven more.

## A year on

The willow tunnel is now the most popular place in the school. The raised beds produced potatoes, beans and a remarkable number of sunflowers. The staff tell us that lunchtimes are noticeably calmer, and that fewer children come in with grazed knees, which we had not expected.

> The quiet children have somewhere to be now. That was the thing I most wanted.

## What we learned

School grounds take heavy wear. We used tougher plants than we would in a garden, protected new hedging with temporary fencing for the first year, and chose bark over grass in the busiest areas. We also wrote a simple maintenance plan that the school and parents can follow without us.

We would like to do more of this kind of work. If your school is thinking about its grounds, we would be glad to hear from you.
