data.title: Reworking a 1970s school playground in Gateshead
data.excerpt: How we turned a tarmac yard into somewhere to play, learn and calm down, with the help of the children who use it.
data.body:
Last summer we finished work on the playground of a primary school in Gateshead. The original was laid in the 1970s and was, in the words of the head teacher, "a car park without the cars". Tarmac from wall to wall, a painted hopscotch, and one tree in a cage.

The school wanted somewhere children could play, learn and calm down, on a budget raised mostly by the parents' association and a local grant. This post is about how we approached it, and what we learned.

Asking the children

We spent two mornings in the school before drawing anything. The children drew their ideal playground, walked us round the current one, and told us where they went when they wanted to be on their own. (Behind the bins, mostly.)

A few things came up again and again:

  • somewhere to hide that was not behind the bins;
  • something to climb that was not the fence;
  • a place to sit with friends out of the wind;
  • more trees, and things growing.

None of that needed expensive play equipment. All of it needed the space to be broken up.

What we built

We kept about half of the tarmac for running games and ball play, because children need open space and the school needed somewhere to line up. The other half we lifted and replaced with:

  1. A low mound, planted with native hedging and small trees, with a willow tunnel through the middle.
  2. Boulders and logs for climbing and sitting, set into bark.
  3. Six raised beds, one for each year group, at child height.
  4. A sheltered seating area under a timber canopy, facing away from the prevailing wind.

The caged tree was freed, and we planted eleven more.

A year on

The willow tunnel is now the most popular place in the school. The raised beds produced potatoes, beans and a remarkable number of sunflowers. The staff tell us that lunchtimes are noticeably calmer, and that fewer children come in with grazed knees, which we had not expected.

The quiet children have somewhere to be now. That was the thing I most wanted.

What we learned

School grounds take heavy wear. We used tougher plants than we would in a garden, protected new hedging with temporary fencing for the first year, and chose bark over grass in the busiest areas. We also wrote a simple maintenance plan that the school and parents can follow without us.

We would like to do more of this kind of work. If your school is thinking about its grounds, we would be glad to hear from you.

examples.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
examples.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
examples.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

## What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

## What it does

- **It keeps moisture in.** A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
- **It suppresses weeds.** Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
- **It feeds the soil.** Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
- **It protects roots** from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
- **It makes a border look finished** , which matters more than people admit.

## When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
2. Water if the soil is dry.
3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

## Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

> Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

- **It keeps moisture in.** A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
- **It suppresses weeds.** Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
- **It feeds the soil.** Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
- **It protects roots** from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
- **It makes a border look finished** , which matters more than people admit.

## When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
2. Water if the soil is dry.
3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

examples.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
examples.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
examples.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

## Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

## A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

## Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

- The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
- The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
- The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

draft.title: The Calder Street courtyard: shade, brick and ferns
draft.excerpt: A small courtyard with three hours of summer sun, planted as a woodland floor rather than a sunny terrace.
draft.body:
The courtyard behind the house on Calder Street gets about three hours of direct sun in midsummer and none at all from November to February. It is enclosed on three sides by brick, two storeys high, and the fourth side is the kitchen.

When the owners first called us, they described it as a cupboard. They had tried pots of lavender and a small olive tree, and both had given up within a season.

## Working with the shade

The first decision was to stop fighting it. Shade is not a problem to be solved in a space like this. It is the character of the place, and some of the best plants we know want exactly these conditions.

So we planted for a woodland floor, not a sunny terrace:

- Ferns, in quantity. Hart's tongue along the base of the walls, soft shield fern in the corners, and a single tree fern by the kitchen window, where it can be seen from the sink.
- Hellebores and epimediums for winter and early spring, when the courtyard most needs something to look at.
- Japanese anemones and hydrangeas for late summer, in white, which glows in low light.
- A multi-stemmed amelanchier as the one tree. It is light enough not to darken the space further, and it flowers, fruits and colours in autumn.

## The brick

The walls were the courtyard's best asset and had been painted cream at some point. We had the paint taken off, which took longer than anything else on the job, and repointed where it needed it. Old brick holds warmth and moss, and against it the green of the ferns looks deeper.

For the floor we used reclaimed setts, laid with wide joints so that moss and a few small ferns can find their way in. It will look better every year.

## Light at night

Because the courtyard is mostly seen from the kitchen, we spent time on the lighting. Two low lights wash up the back wall, and one picks out the tree fern from below. In winter, when the garden is dark by four, it gives the kitchen a view rather than a black window.

> It doesn't feel like a cupboard any more. It feels like somewhere we chose.

## Looking after it

A shady courtyard is easy to maintain if it is planted well. There is no lawn and very little to deadhead. The main jobs are cutting back old fern fronds in March, mulching with leaf mould in autumn, and keeping an eye on watering in the first summer, since walls cast a rain shadow as well as a sun one.

We left the owners with a one-page calendar of what to do and when. It fits on the fridge, which is where, we are told, it lives.

draft.title: Rain gardens for ordinary front gardens
draft.excerpt: A planted hollow that catches water from a roof and lets it sink in slowly. Simpler than it sounds, and it works in more places than you would think.
draft.body:
Most front gardens in the North East were paved at some point in the last thirty years, usually to park a car. It made sense at the time. The trouble is that all the rain that used to soak into that soil now runs straight into the drains, and in a heavy storm the drains cannot cope.

A rain garden is one small way to put some of that back. It sounds technical, but it is really just a planted dip that catches water from a roof or a path and lets it sink in slowly.

## How it works

You disconnect a downpipe, or part of one, and send the water across the surface into a shallow planted hollow. The hollow fills in a downpour and drains within a day or two. The plants are chosen to cope with both: wet feet for a while, then dry spells in summer.

The aim is not to hold water permanently. If it is still standing after forty-eight hours, the soil needs opening up or the hollow needs to be bigger.

## Will it work in my garden?

It works in more places than people expect. A few things to check first:

- It should sit at least a few metres from the house, so water is not sent towards the foundations.
- Very heavy clay drains slowly. You can still do it, but the hollow needs to be wider and shallower, with grit dug into the base.
- Do not build one over a septic tank, a soakaway or a cellar.

A simple test: dig a hole about thirty centimetres deep, fill it with water, and see how long it takes to empty. Under a day is ideal. Two days is workable.

## What to plant

We use a mix of plants that cope with both wet and dry, and keep the wettest-loving ones in the bottom of the dip.

- **In the base:** purple loosestrife, meadowsweet, the smaller sedges and flag iris if there is room.
- **On the slopes:** hardy geraniums, astrantia, sanguisorba and some of the taller grasses.
- **Around the rim:** anything that suits the rest of the garden, as this part stays relatively dry.

## Is it worth it?

One rain garden will not stop a street from flooding. But it does take a real share of the water off a single roof, it looks far better than a gully, and it brings insects and birds into a part of the garden that usually has none.

We have built several now, from a small one beside a terraced house in Heaton to a long swale along a school drive. If you are thinking about one, we are happy to come and have a look.

examples.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
examples.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
examples.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

## What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

## What it does

- **It keeps moisture in.** A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
- **It suppresses weeds.** Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
- **It feeds the soil.** Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
- **It protects roots** from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
- **It makes a border look finished** , which matters more than people admit.

## When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
2. Water if the soil is dry.
3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

## Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

> Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

examples.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
examples.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
examples.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

## Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

## A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

## Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

- The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
- The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
- The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

## How it has settled

Three summers on, the meadow is starting to find its balance. The first year was mostly annual cornfield flowers, as it always is. Since then the perennials have taken over: knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, field scabious and a good deal of yellow rattle, which keeps the grass in check.

> We walk down to the bottom most evenings now. We never used to go past the washing line.

Slopes put many people off, but they make some of the most rewarding gardens to design. The changes in level give you views, shelter and a sense of journey that a flat plot cannot.

draft.title: Why we start every project with a site walk
draft.excerpt: Before any drawings, we spend two hours walking the garden with the people who use it. Here is why.
draft.body:
Every Northfold project starts the same way. Before any drawings, before any talk of budgets or planting lists, we walk the site with the people who use it. It usually takes about two hours. It is the most useful two hours of the whole job.

## What we are looking for

Some of it is technical. We look at the soil, the drainage, where the water goes after rain, which way the wind comes from and where the frost sits. We note every tree, every level change and every view worth keeping or hiding.

But most of it is about people. Where do you stand when you come out of the back door? Where does the sun reach at six in the evening in June? Where do the children actually play, as opposed to where the lawn is? Which corner do you avoid?

examples.title: Mulch, and why we talk about it so much
examples.excerpt: If we could persuade every gardener to do one thing, it would be this. What mulch does, and how to use it.
examples.body:
Anyone who has worked with us will know that we talk about mulch a great deal. Clients have been known to roll their eyes. We are not going to stop, because if we could persuade every gardener in the country to do one thing, this would be it.

## What mulch is

Mulch is any layer of material spread over the surface of the soil. It can be organic, like compost, leaf mould, bark or well-rotted manure, or inorganic, like gravel or slate. Here we mean the organic kind, which feeds the soil as well as covering it.

## What it does

- **It keeps moisture in.** A mulched border can need half the watering of a bare one in a dry spell.
- **It suppresses weeds.** Not completely, but enough that weeding becomes a gentle job rather than a battle.
- **It feeds the soil.** Worms pull the mulch down into the ground over the year, improving its structure and fertility without you having to dig.
- **It protects roots** from hard frost in winter and heat in summer.
- **It makes a border look finished** , which matters more than people admit.

## When and how

The best times are autumn and early spring, when the soil is moist and not frozen. Never mulch dry soil; you will lock the dryness in.

1. Weed the border first, especially perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed.
2. Water if the soil is dry.
3. Spread the mulch about five centimetres deep. Less does little. Much more can smother small plants.
4. Keep it a hand's width away from the stems of shrubs and trees, so they do not rot.

## Which mulch

Home-made compost is best if you have enough, which most people do not. Leaf mould is wonderful for shady and woodland planting, and easy to make if you have a tree or two: bag the leaves in autumn, poke some holes in the bags, and wait eighteen months.

Bought composted bark is a good all-rounder. Avoid fresh wood chip on borders; it takes nitrogen from the soil as it breaks down. It is fine on paths.

We are cautious about mushroom compost around acid-loving plants, since it is often limy, and about manure that is not well rotted, which can scorch roots.

> Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the plants.

That is an old saying and not one of ours, but we have yet to find a better summary. If you do nothing else in the garden this autumn, mulch.

examples.title: A hillside garden in the Tyne Valley
examples.excerpt: An eleven-metre drop, a path that zigzags down it, and a meadow that is finally finding its balance.
examples.body:
The garden above the village of Riding Mill falls about eleven metres from the back of the house to the bottom boundary, over a distance of not much more than forty. When we first visited, most of it was rough grass that the owners mowed, with some difficulty, using a strimmer on a rope.

They wanted to be able to walk down it. They wanted somewhere flat to eat. And they wanted it to feel like part of the valley rather than a suburban garden dropped onto a hill.

## Paths before planting

On a slope like this, the paths are the design. We spent longer on the route down than on anything else, walking it again and again with canes and string until it felt natural.

The final path zigzags gently across the hill, never steeper than a comfortable stroll, with three landings where the view opens up. It is surfaced in local whinstone chippings, held in place by oak edging, with steps only where the slope demanded them.

## A flat place to sit

The one level terrace sits just below the house, built up on a dry stone wall. We used stone from a collapsed field wall on the property, rebuilt by a local waller over three weeks. It cost more than a concrete block wall with a stone face, but it will last longer, it drains better, and within a year it was full of ferns and wall pennywort.

## Planting the slope

Below the terrace, the planting gets steadily wilder as you go down. Near the house it is fairly ordered: grasses, salvias, nepeta and a few shrubs. Halfway down it becomes a meadow, sown with a native seed mix suited to the valley's thin, acidic soil. At the bottom, along the boundary, we planted a mixed hedge of hawthorn, hazel, holly and field maple, and a small group of birch.

- The meadow is cut once a year, in late August, and the hay removed.
- The hedge is cut every other year, in late winter, on alternate sides.
- The borders by the house are cut back in February.

That is close to the whole maintenance plan, which was the point.

## How it has settled

Three summers on, the meadow is starting to find its balance. The first year was mostly annual cornfield flowers, as it always is. Since then the perennials have taken over: knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, field scabious and a good deal of yellow rattle, which keeps the grass in check.

> We walk down to the bottom most evenings now. We never used to go past the washing line.

Slopes put many people off, but they make some of the most rewarding gardens to design. The changes in level give you views, shelter and a sense of journey that a flat plot cannot.
